AO 22 Rockwood & Green 10e

Diaphyseal Fractures of the Radius & Ulna

Forearm shaft fractures · Both-bone · Nightstick · Monteggia · Galeazzi

Epidemiology & Mechanism

Incidence

  • Bimodal: young adults (high-energy) and elderly (low-energy/osteoporotic)
  • Both-bone fractures: ~50% of adult forearm shaft fractures
  • Isolated ulna (nightstick): most common isolated forearm fracture; direct blow
  • Isolated radius: uncommon without DRUJ disruption (Galeazzi)
  • Male predominance in high-energy mechanisms

Mechanism

  • Direct blow → isolated ulna shaft (nightstick)
  • FOOSH → both-bone or Galeazzi
  • High-energy (MVA, fall from height) → comminuted both-bone
  • Hyperpronation / FOOSH → Monteggia type I
  • Forced pronation + valgus stress → Monteggia type II

Clinical Evaluation

History & Exam

  • Mechanism (direct vs. indirect), dominant extremity, occupation
  • Open wound: timing, degree of contamination
  • Swelling, deformity, ecchymosis over forearm
  • Examine DRUJ: point tenderness, piano-key sign → Galeazzi
  • Examine elbow + radial head: any isolated ulna fracture → rule out Monteggia
  • Complete neurovascular exam: radial, ulnar, median, AIN, PIN
  • Compartment assessment if severe swelling

Imaging

  • AP and lateral forearm (full length)
  • Always obtain elbow AND wrist radiographs in same series
  • Radiocapitellar line on lateral: must bisect capitellum
  • DRUJ: ulnar variance, styloid fracture, joint widening >2 mm
  • CT if articular involvement, complex pattern, or unclear anatomy
Galeazzi radiographic signs:
1. Radius fracture at middle-distal third junction
2. Ulnar styloid fracture (TFCC avulsion)
3. DRUJ widening >2 mm (AP) or incongruence (lateral)

Special Fracture Patterns

Nightstick Fracture
Isolated ulna; radius intact. <50% displacement AND <10° angulation → functional brace. >50% displacement or >10° angulation → ORIF.
Monteggia
Ulna shaft fracture + radial head dislocation. Must rule out in any isolated ulna fracture. Adults: nearly always ORIF ulna ± address radial head.
Galeazzi
Radius shaft fracture + DRUJ disruption. "Fracture of necessity" in adults — always operative. ORIF radius; intraoperative DRUJ assessment mandatory.

Osseous Anatomy & Biomechanics

  • Radius & ulna connected by: PRUJ, interosseous membrane (IOM), DRUJ — function as a ring
  • Radial bow: peak lateral bow ~60% of length from radial head — critical for forearm rotation; must be restored surgically
  • IOM central band: transmits ~60% of axial load; oblique from proximal-ulnar to distal-radial
  • Ulna: subcutaneous border palpable throughout; minimal soft tissue coverage
  • Forearm rotation: 150° total arc (75° pronation, 75° supination); any loss significantly impairs function
Deforming forces on radius: Supinator inserts on proximal radius → supinates proximal fragment. Pronator teres (mid-shaft) and pronator quadratus (distal) pronate distal fragment. Fracture level relative to PT insertion determines rotational deformity of each fragment.

Anterior (Volar) Forearm Anatomy

Key Anterior Structures

  • Radial artery: medial to brachioradialis; key landmark in Henry approach; retract radially with BR proximally, medially distally
  • Median nerve: enters between PT heads; gives off AIN; not in direct Henry dissection plane but close proximally
  • AIN: motor to FPL, FDP (index/long), pronator quadratus; arises from median nerve at PT level; at risk in deep proximal Henry dissection
  • Ulnar nerve & artery: travel together deep to FCU; protect during ulnar approach

Key Anterior Relationships

  • Pronator teres insertion: mid-lateral radius — must elevate for middle-third radius exposure (Henry)
  • Bicipital aponeurosis (lacertus fibrosus): protects brachial artery & median nerve at elbow level
  • Arcade of Frohse: fibrous arch of supinator; PIN traverses through it; forearm supination opens arcade
  • FDS arch: AIN passes beneath at its origin
  • Leash of Henry (radial recurrent vessels): must ligate for proximal radius exposure

Posterior (Dorsal) Forearm Anatomy

Key Posterior Structures

  • PIN (posterior interosseous nerve): deep radial nerve branch; enters supinator at Arcade of Frohse; exits distal supinator; primary nerve at risk in Thompson approach
  • Superficial radial nerve: sensory only; beneath brachioradialis; exits at distal forearm; at risk in distal lateral dissection
  • Anconeus: landmark for ulnar approach; triangular muscle between ECU and FCU

Thompson Interval

  • Proximal: between ECRB (lateral) and EDC (medial)
  • Distal: between EPL and EDC
  • APL and EPB cross the operative field obliquely — must retract or work around
  • Supinate forearm to rotate PIN posteriorly (away from field) during proximal exposure
  • Pronator teres insertion visible at lateral radius in middle third

Operative vs. Non-Operative Indications

Non-Operative

  • Nightstick (isolated ulna): <50% displacement AND <10° angulation → short arm functional brace × 6–8 weeks; weekly radiographs × 3 weeks
  • Pediatric (under 10 years): most shaft fractures → closed reduction + casting
  • Medically unfit patients with non-displaced fractures
Adult both-bone forearm fractures are ALMOST ALWAYS operative. Non-operative in adults → unacceptably high malunion rate; cannot maintain reduction.

Operative Indications

  • All both-bone forearm fractures in adults
  • Isolated ulna with >50% displacement OR >10° angulation
  • All Galeazzi fractures in adults ("fracture of necessity")
  • All Monteggia fracture-dislocations in adults
  • Open fractures (emergency I&D + fixation)
  • Segmental fractures
  • Neurovascular compromise
  • Failed closed reduction in pediatric cases

ORIF — Plate & Screw Fixation

Standard: 3.5 mm DCP or LCP — minimum 6 cortices (3 screws) each side of fracture; 7–8 cortices in osteoporotic bone. Both bones fixed independently through separate incisions.

Plate Selection by Fracture Type

PatternImplant
Simple (A)3.5 mm DCP; lag screw + neutralization
Wedge (B)3.5 mm DCP or LCP; interfragmentary screw if reducible
Comminuted (C)3.5 mm LCP bridge plate; do not compress comminution zone
OsteoporoticLCP throughout; consider longer plate
MonteggiaPre-contoured proximal ulna LCP
Galeazzi3.5 mm DCP/LCP radius; DRUJ pinning if unstable

Plate Positioning Principles

  • Radius: volar surface preferred (tension side in supination); Henry approach; dorsal via Thompson for proximal third
  • Ulna: dorsomedial (compression) surface; avoids subcutaneous prominence
  • Restore radial bow: use contralateral radiograph as template; critical for forearm rotation recovery
  • Lag screw first for oblique/spiral fractures, then neutralization plate
  • Bridge plate for comminution: restore length and alignment without disturbing zone

Intramedullary Nailing

  • Limited role in adults; may be used for segmental fractures, re-fractures through plate holes
  • Cannot reliably restore radial bow → higher malunion/nonunion rates than plating
  • Semi-rigid (flexible) nailing: pediatric ages 6–14 years — standard of care

Galeazzi-Specific Management

  1. ORIF radius with 3.5 mm plate (restores length and alignment)
  2. Assess DRUJ stability intraoperatively: stress test in neutral and supination
  3. If stable: long-arm cast in supination × 4–6 weeks
  4. If unstable: trans-articular K-wire (DRUJ pinning) × 4 weeks, forearm in supination, OR TFCC direct repair
  5. Ulnar styloid base fracture = TFCC avulsion → repair if DRUJ remains unstable after radius fixation

Monteggia-Specific Management

  1. ORIF ulna: restore length, alignment, angulation → radial head usually reduces concentrically
  2. Confirm radial head reduction with fluoroscopy: radiocapitellar line must bisect capitellum on lateral
  3. Irreducible radial head: explore for soft tissue interposition (annular ligament), residual ulna malalignment
  4. Bado II: assess coronoid; ORIF coronoid if significant fragment (Jupiter IIA/B)
  5. Radial head fracture (Bado IV): ORIF or arthroplasty if unreconstructable
  6. Chronic missed Monteggia: ulnar osteotomy + annular ligament reconstruction

Postoperative Protocol

PhaseTimingActivity
Immobilization0–2 weeksSplint; wound healing; finger ROM
Early ROM2–6 weeksActive forearm rotation, elbow, wrist ROM; no resistance
Strengthening6–12 weeksProgressive resistance once radiographic callus visible
Full activity4–6 monthsCortical bridging on 3 of 4 cortices confirmed
Galeazzi exception: Long-arm cast × 4 weeks (with/without K-wire), then pin removal, then ROM.

Direct Ulnar Approach

Interval

  • Between FCU (anterior — ulnar nerve) and ECU (posterior — PIN)
  • Anconeus: proximally retracted with ECU
  • Subcutaneous border of ulna — palpable throughout; guides incision

Steps

  1. Longitudinal incision along subcutaneous border of ulna
  2. Develop interval between ECU (posterior) and FCU (anterior)
  3. Elevate periosteum subperiosteally from ulna
  4. Protect ulnar nerve running beneath FCU in distal two-thirds
  5. Protect dorsal cutaneous branch of ulnar nerve (exits 5–8 cm proximal to ulnar styloid)
Ulnar nerve: enters between FCU heads; runs on FDP deep to FCU; at risk if dissection drifts anterior in distal forearm.

Volar Henry Approach to the Radius

Interval

  • Between brachioradialis (BR) [radial nerve] and FCR [median nerve]
  • Radial artery in the interval: retract radially with BR proximally; medially at wrist
  • Lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve: protect along lateral wound edge

Steps

  1. Longitudinal incision: bicipital tuberosity to radial styloid (full or partial as needed)
  2. Identify and protect lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve
  3. Develop BR–FCR interval; identify radial artery
  4. Ligate leash of Henry (radial recurrent vessels) for proximal exposure
  5. Middle third: pronate forearm; elevate PT insertion from lateral radius
  6. Proximal third: supinate forearm; supinator elevated subperiosteally; identify AIN
  7. Distal third: supinate; elevate FPL and pronator quadratus subperiosteally
AIN protection (proximal Henry): Stay on bone during periosteal elevation; identify nerve before placing deep retractors over proximal radius. AIN exits median nerve at PT level and runs on interosseous membrane.

Dorsal Thompson Approach to the Radius

Interval

  • Proximal: between ECRB (lateral) and EDC (medial)
  • Distal: between EPL and EDC
  • APL and EPB cross field obliquely — retract distally or work around

Step Walkthrough — Thompson Approach

Navigate through operative steps using the dots.

PIN Protection — Critical Points (Thompson Approach):
• Fully supinate forearm during proximal exposure — rotates PIN posteriorly away from field
• Identify PIN before splitting supinator
• Never place blind retractors around proximal radius without PIN identification
• Arcade of Frohse: tight fibrous arch may need release
• Once PIN identified, forearm can be carefully pronated for distal exposure

Overview

Nonunion
~2–5% with modern plating. Risk: inadequate fixation, infection, bone gap, smoking, NSAIDs.
Malunion
Loss of radial bow → rotation deficit. Angular deformity. Critical to restore anatomy intraoperatively.
Radioulnar Synostosis
0.5–9%. Risk: crush injury, single incision, periosteal stripping, delay to fixation.

Acute Compartment Syndrome — Forearm

  • Threshold: compartment pressure >30 mmHg or delta-p (diastolic BP − compartment pressure) <30 mmHg
  • Clinical: pain out of proportion, pain with passive stretch, tense compartment, paresthesias, paralysis (late)
  • Fasciotomy: single volar incision (Henry) for volar compartment; separate dorsal incision for dorsal compartment; carpal tunnel release distally as needed
  • Both-bone fractures + vascular injury = highest risk group
Volkmann ischemic contracture: Late sequela of untreated forearm compartment syndrome — irreversible muscle necrosis → flexion contracture of wrist and fingers. Prevention is the goal; once established, treatment requires extensive reconstruction.
